title: Build Resilient Insurance Print and Mail Operations
summary: Explore ways to manage insurance renewal peaks, staffing gaps and everyday mail disruptions with backup capacity, flexible production and outsourcing.
body_markdown:
## The pressure you’re under


A mailroom is temporarily closed during an office move, or a network outage interrupts file delivery.


By morning, policyholder notices and billing correspondence are accumulating, even though the next renewal cycle is still approaching. A storm or catastrophic event can create the same pressure on a much larger scale.


Insurance operations have to accommodate both kinds of volume: the peaks you can predict and the ones you can't.


Renewal and premium cycles create recurring production demand. Catastrophic events (CAT events) can create sudden spikes. Policy issuance, billing, claims and customer-service activity continue alongside both.


Some communications also carry jurisdiction- and product-specific requirements. For cancellation, non-renewal, lapse and claims correspondence, confirm applicable notice timing, content and delivery rules with your legal or compliance team rather than assuming one national mailing rule applies everywhere.


That combination makes excess capacity valuable, but expensive to maintain year-round.


Should you own enough production capacity for the worst week of the year? Not necessarily.


There are three ways to reduce the risk, depending on where you are today: establish a continuity path, use outside production to absorb peaks, or move production offsite entirely.

## 1. Business continuity: when policyholder mail cannot stop with the facility


Business continuity plans often focus first on claims systems, contact centers, policy administration and IT.


Physical communications deserve a place in that plan too.


An office move, network outage, cyber event, equipment failure or staffing disruption can interrupt production while policyholder activity continues. Depending on the line of business and jurisdiction, certain cancellation, non-renewal, lapse or other policyholder notices can have specific timing or content requirements.


Not every disruption is a disaster. An office relocation, an internet outage, planned maintenance, an employee on parental leave or an unexpected staffing gap can interrupt everyday mailing just as effectively. During a catastrophic event, those challenges may become more widespread.


A mail continuity arrangement establishes an alternate production path before that happens.


Critical jobs, templates and procedures can be identified in advance. Secure file-transfer methods can be established and tested. Activation responsibilities can be documented. Alternate production capacity can then be used when the normal site cannot operate.


For insurers, testing is particularly important. A continuity provider that theoretically has capacity is different from one that has already validated your workflow.


Ask how quickly jobs can be activated, which communications will receive priority, how current document versions are maintained and how your team will see production status.


This model fits insurers with an established document-production operation that still makes strategic and financial sense.


The objective isn't to replace it. It's to make sure one facility doesn't determine whether policyholder communications move.


**Related reading:**[Explore business continuity solutions](https://www.pitneybowes.com/us/campaign/business-continuity.html)


## 2. Hybrid onsite/offsite: flexing from renewals to CAT volume


Insurance has an unusual capacity-planning challenge because it combines two fundamentally different kinds of peaks.


The first is predictable. Renewal seasons, premium billing schedules and policy cycles can create recurring surges that operations teams know are coming.


The second isn't. A CAT event can change claims and policyholder communication volumes almost overnight. CAT volume should not have to compete with everyday policyholder mail for production capacity.


Sizing an internal operation for both scenarios can leave an insurer carrying expensive excess capacity for much of the year.


A hybrid model creates a pressure-release valve.


Keep the work that makes sense onsite and route defined overflow externally. That might mean sending renewal overflow offsite during peak periods, moving a particular line of business to external production, or activating incremental capacity when claims volumes spike.


You don't have to outsource the entire operation to gain outsourced capacity.


**Related reading:**[Ideas for avoiding mail center bottlenecks](https://www.pitneybowes.com/us/blog/avoid-mail-center-challenges.html)


The challenge is making two production environments behave like one.


Forms and templates need strong version control. Data must be protected. Output and quality standards should remain consistent. Reporting should tell operations which site handled each job without creating a reconciliation exercise.


When those controls are established in advance, external capacity becomes something operations can activate, not something procurement has to find during a crisis.


## 3. Full outsourcing: separating insurance operations from print operations


Insurers are in the business of underwriting risk, administering policies, servicing customers and handling claims.


Operating production equipment is necessary for many organizations, but it isn't necessarily differentiating.


Full outsourcing changes that equation.


Instead of maintaining printers, inserters, production shifts and excess capacity internally, approved data and documents move into an external production workflow. The provider handles printing, inserting and mailing while the insurer maintains governance and visibility.


This can make costs more predictable while reducing equipment, staffing and floor-space requirements. It can also give the organization access to production expertise and capacity across multiple lines of business.


But insurers should not interpret outsourcing as giving up control. Quite the opposite: governance becomes more important.


Service levels need to reflect the urgency of different notice types. Document-control procedures need to prevent an outdated form from entering production. Reporting should establish what was produced and when. Security controls should match the sensitivity of the information being processed.


And compliance requirements must be evaluated at the appropriate level. Notice requirements vary by state, product and communication type, so production workflows need enough flexibility to support those differences rather than assuming one national rule applies to every notice.


The best outsourcing model therefore doesn't simply remove equipment. It gives insurance operations a production capability that can scale without requiring them to operate the infrastructure behind it.
